sources.claim: Real game engines build an actor's visibility bounds from simplified geometric shapes (a sphere and a box), not the real mesh, specifically to make per-frame visibility testing fast
sources.value: "The bounds of an Actor is made up of two parts: a sphere and a box... The bounding sphere enables fast collision detection through simple distance calculations, while the bounding box is a closer match to the shape of the object and provides more accurate results."
sources.title: Visibility and Occlusion Culling in Unreal Engine

sources.title: Occlusion culling
sources.note: Directly fetched and confirmed live. deliverables.text: For each of the three representative props (Appendix B), a complete volume AND surface area calculation of the prop's real shape, decomposed into its component solids (a cylinder plus a cone, or a cylinder plus a square pyramid), shown step by step.
For each prop, the bounding sphere's volume (Option A) and the wasted volume (sphere volume minus the prop's real volume from D1), per prop and as a scene-wide total using Appendix C's prop counts.

For each prop, the bounding capsule's volume (Option B -- a cylinder spanning the prop's full height at the prop's own widest radius, capped by two hemispheres) and its wasted volume, per prop and as a scene-wide total.
Using Appendix D's cost figures, each option's total added per-frame cost in milliseconds, shown step by step for both options, with the margin between them.

A one-paragraph written recommendation naming which bounding-shape policy has the lower total per-frame cost, and explicitly addressing which of Appendix D's cost figures the recommendation is most sensitive to.

balance.argument_a: Option A (single bounding sphere) escalates only its CPU culling-test cost: 1,800 tested props/frame × 0.0005 ms [MA7] = 0.900 ms. A's case is that this is the cheapest possible per-object test, full stop -- a single distance-squared-vs-radius-squared comparison, the fastest class of geometric check available, and that cost scales linearly and predictably with scene density no matter how the props are shaped.
balance.argument_b: Option B (bounding capsule) costs more per test -- 1,800 × 0.0015 ms [MA8] = 2.700 ms of CPU cost, three times A's -- but wastes dramatically less bounding volume: summed across all three prop types and 600 copies each, Option A's spheres waste roughly 108.2 million liters of bounding volume scene-wide, versus Option B's capsules at roughly 306,500 liters -- a difference of two and a half orders of magnitude. At the case's stated wasted-volume-to-render-cost conversion [MA9], that wasted volume adds 2.163 ms of render/overdraw cost to Option A versus just 0.006 ms to Option B. B's real, quantitative case is that this render-cost term, not the CPU-test cost, is where the actual frame-budget damage lives for long, thin props specifically.
balance.margin_basis: cost(option) = tested_props_total × per_test_cost_ms(option) + total_wasted_volume_L(option) × render_cost_per_L [MA9]. tested_props_total = 1,800 (Appendix C). cost(A) = 1,800×0.0005 + 108,172,271×0.00000002 = 0.900 + 2.163 = 3.063 ms. cost(B) = 1,800×0.0015 + 306,525×0.00000002 = 2.700 + 0.006 = 2.706 ms (winner, lower cost). margin = |3.063−2.706| / 2.706 × 100 = 0.357/2.706 × 100 = 13.2%. This is within SPEC §2's 20% cap. NOTE: every input to this calculation (Appendix B's decorative-component dimensions, Appendix C's prop counts, and all three of Appendix D's cost figures MA7-MA9) is a stated Modeling Assumption except the lamppost height range [S1] and the pipe diameter [S2] -- this margin is a designed property of those chosen values, not an empirical finding about any real game engine's actual measured frame cost.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public source publishes an exact per-object bounding-sphere test cost (MA7). Tier 2 P5 found this dial genuinely unstable: -50% FLIPS the winner to A (margin 3.5%); +50% breaches the 20% cap (29.8%, B still wins).

No public source publishes an exact per-object bounding-capsule test cost (MA8). Tier 2 P5 found this is the case's most flip-sensitive dial: -50% breaches the cap (125.9%, B still wins); +50% FLIPS the winner to A and breaches the cap (32.4%).

No public source ties wasted bounding volume to a millisecond rendering cost (MA9) -- this is the case's central constructed conversion. Tier 2 P5 found this dial genuinely unstable: -50% FLIPS the winner to A and breaches the cap (36.4%); +50% breaches the cap in the other direction (53.0%, B still wins).
